claims.text: The as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type alloy has a high density of microstructural defects and substantial lattice strain.
The as-deposited alloy has an inhomogeneous magnetic-exchange landscape.
Defects, strain, and compositional inhomogeneities produce a broad distribution of magnetic exchange interactions.
The distribution of magnetic exchange interactions governs both the sharpness and hysteresis of the magnetocaloric response during low-field cycling.
Sub-recrystallization annealing under an inert atmosphere will relieve residual stress and reduce defect density.
Reducing defects will make lattice strain more homogeneous.
Reducing defects and homogenizing strain will narrow the distribution of magnetic exchange parameters.
Homogenization of exchange interactions will reduce magnetic pinning.
Reduced magnetic pinning will lower hysteretic losses.
Annealing-induced homogenization will sharpen the magnetocaloric entropy-change profile.
Changes in the shape of the magnetic entropy-change curve can alter the effective working-temperature range or refrigerant capacity.
The annealed sample will show lower coercivity and reduced magnetic hysteresis relative to the as-deposited sample.
The annealed sample will have a less sharp and possibly slightly broadened magnetic entropy-change-versus-temperature curve.
The as-deposited baseline has a broad, hysteretic magnetocaloric response with a sharp entropy-change peak.
The prediction is restricted to low-field cycles spanning the alloy's magnetostructural-transition range and to samples with comparable composition and cooling history.

Failure to obtain both a statistically significant hysteresis reduction and a discernible entropy-profile modification after verified defect reduction would falsify the proposed governing role of disorder.

contradictions.description: The mechanism predicts that annealing sharpens the entropy-change profile, whereas the predicted outcome says that annealing makes the profile less sharp and possibly broader.
The baseline is described simultaneously as broad and as having a sharp entropy-change peak, making the predicted transition to a less-sharp or broadened curve ambiguous.
